Dash
dăsh
v. (to strike violently against; to shatter by striking; rendering Hebrew naphats, nagaph, and ratash, Greek proskopto)
Middle English dasshen, to strike, of Scandinavian origin. In the Psalms it is what the Messiah does to rebel nations and what the angels prevent happening to a foot.

Biblical Definition

The Father to the Son: “Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” (Psa 2:9). The angels' charge: “They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone” (Psa 91:12), which the devil quoted to Christ on the pinnacle (Mat 4:6; Luk 4:11). Of Judah: “I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the LORD: I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy” (Jer 13:14). Elisha wept because Hazael would “dash their children” (2Ki 8:12), and the Medes' bows “shall dash the young men to pieces” (Isa 13:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dash as to strike suddenly or violently; to break by collision; to throw with violence.

expand to see more

DASH, v.t. To strike suddenly or violently, whether throwing or falling; as, to dash one stone against another.

2. To strike and bruise or break; to break by collision.

3. To throw water suddenly, in separate portions.

4. To sprinkle; to confound; to abash; to depress.

Key Scripture

Psa 2:9 — "Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel."

Psa 91:12 — "They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone."

Mat 4:6 — "And saith unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone."

Jer 13:14 — "And I will dash them one against another, even the fathers and the sons together, saith the LORD: I will not pity, nor spare, nor have mercy, but destroy them."

2Ki 8:12 — "And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child."

Modern Corruption

Christ is preached without a rod, and the devil quoted the psalm about the foot with a clause left out.

expand to see more

Psalm 2 is quoted three times in Revelation, and each time it is the rod of iron and the dashing of the nations that is quoted (Rev 2:27; 12:5; 19:15). The Christ of the modern pulpit has no rod. He invites, He accompanies, He affirms, and the psalm the apostles prayed in Acts 4 — “Why did the heathen rage?” — ends with kings kissing the Son lest He be angry and they perish from the way. A gospel that cannot say “thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” has no reason left to say “Kiss the Son.” The mercy is offered because the rod is real.

Matthew 4:6 is the devil's exegesis. He quoted Psalm 91:11–12 accurately as far as it went, and omitted “to keep thee in all thy ways” — the clause that made the promise a promise to a man walking in God's ways and not to a man throwing himself off a roof to test it. Every abuse of a promise since has used the same method: the text quoted, the condition dropped. The Lord answered with another text, and the lesson is that Scripture is not safe in the hands of anyone who will not read it whole.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naphats (H5310), to shatter, break in pieces; nagaph (H5062), to strike, stumble; ratash (H7376), to dash in pieces; Greek proskopto (G4350), to strike against.

expand to see more

Hebrew naphats (H5310) — to dash in pieces, shatter; Psalm 2:9, Jeremiah 13:14, Judges 7:19.

Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to strike, stumble; Psalm 91:12; ratash (H7376), 2 Kings 8:12, Isaiah 13:18.

Greek proskopto (G4350) — to strike against, stumble; Matthew 4:6, Luke 4:11, John 11:9–10.

Usage

"“Thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” — the rod that makes the mercy urgent."

"“Lest thou dash thy foot against a stone” — quoted by the devil, minus a clause."

"“I will dash them one against another” — judgment told without softening."
